details:
**Four Sights**
While Prince Siddhartha Gautama was growing up, his father, King Suddhodana, kept him sheltered in the palace. On trips outside it, Siddhartha saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic (monk). Shaken by the reality of suffering, he made the "Great Renunciation," leaving his wife Yasodhara and newborn son Rahula (whose name means "fetter") and riding off on his horse Kanthaka, which is said to have died of a broken heart afterward.

**Bodhi tree**
The sacred fig tree at Bodh Gaya under which Siddhartha meditated until he attained enlightenment and became the Buddha ("Awakened One"). Tradition says he then spent seven weeks (49 days) meditating nearby, during which the serpent king Mucalinda coiled around him and spread his hoods to shelter him from a storm.

**Deer Park at Sarnath (First Sermon)**
The Buddha's first sermon after enlightenment, delivered near Benares (Varanasi) to the five ascetics who had been his companions, including Kondanna (Kaundinya) and Assaji. Called "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma," it laid out the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way, and the five ascetics became his first disciples and the first arhats.

**Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path**
The core of the Buddha's teaching: life involves suffering (dukkha); suffering arises from craving; suffering can end; and the way to end it is the Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration). Following it leads to nirvana and release from samsara, the cycle of rebirth.

**Middle Way**
The Buddha's teaching that the path to liberation avoids both indulgence in sensual pleasure and extreme self-denial. He arrived at it after years of severe asceticism nearly starved him to death.

**Queen Maya's dream of the white elephant**
Before Siddhartha was conceived, his mother, Queen Maya, dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks entered her right side. He was born in the Lumbini grove in present-day Nepal, and Theravada Buddhists celebrate his birth, enlightenment, and death on the holiday of Vesak.

**Flower Sermon**
A wordless teaching in which the Buddha simply held up a white flower before his assembled disciples at Vulture Peak. Only Mahakashyapa understood and smiled, and this mind-to-mind transmission is regarded as the origin of Zen Buddhism.

**Mara and the earth-touching mudra**
Before his enlightenment, the demon Mara attacked Siddhartha with armies and tempted him with his daughters. When Mara challenged his right to enlightenment, Siddhartha touched the ground and called the Earth to witness. This earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudra) is one of the most common poses in Buddha statues.

**Fire Sermon**
A sermon that begins "All is burning," in which the Buddha teaches that the senses, the mind, and their objects are aflame with greed, hatred, and delusion. By growing disenchanted with them, a disciple achieves liberation.

**Parable of the poisoned arrow**
The Buddha's explanation for refusing to answer metaphysical questions (the "unanswered questions"). A man shot with a poisoned arrow who refuses treatment until he knows who shot it, and what the bow and arrow were made of, will die before learning the answers. Likewise, speculation distracts from ending suffering.

**Angulimala**
A notorious bandit who killed travelers and wore their fingers as a necklace, having been told by his teacher to collect a thousand fingers. The Buddha stopped him before he could kill his own mother, and Angulimala converted and became a monk.

**Last meal from Cunda**
The Buddha's final meal was given by Cunda, a blacksmith. It was a dish called sukara-maddava, interpreted as either pork or a food enjoyed by pigs, such as mushrooms. He fell ill afterward and passed into parinirvana (final nirvana) at Kushinagar.

**Anatta (Anattalakkhana Sutta)**
The Buddha's second discourse, given to the same five ascetics, teaching that form, feeling, perception, and the other aggregates are "not-self" (anatta). On hearing it, the five became arhats.

**Bamiyan Buddhas and other statues**
Two giant Buddha statues carved into a cliff in Afghanistan's Bamiyan valley were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001. Other famous images include the Daibutsu (Great Buddha) at Todai-ji in Nara, Japan, a stone Buddha head entwined in tree roots at Wat Mahathat in Ayutthaya, Thailand, and a statue standing in Hussain Sagar lake in Hyderabad. In the Chinese painting The Vinegar Tasters, the Buddha wears a bitter expression, Confucius a sour one, and Laozi a smile.

**Thirty-two marks of a great man**
Physical signs said to distinguish a Buddha, such as forty even teeth, a lion-like body, and wheels imprinted on the soles of the feet. At Siddhartha's birth, seers predicted he would become either a universal monarch or a world-saving spiritual teacher.
